concepts.summary: Almost everywhere, the sun's crossing of the sky is imagined as a journey with a vehicle and a driver: a boat, a chariot, a golden cup, a team of horses, an escort of the dead. The harder question is the return trip, since the sun sets in the west and rises again in the east, and each tradition must decide how it gets back. Horse-drawn suns in Greek, Vedic and Norse sources are often traced to a shared Indo-European inheritance; Egypt's boat suits a river civilisation, and the Aztec and Polynesian versions are clearly independent. Similar skies prompt similar solutions.

versions.title: The Two Boats of Ra
versions.teaser: Ra sails the sky by day and the underworld by night.
versions.text:
Ra does not drive; he sails. By day he crosses the sky in the day-barque, the ‘boat of millions of years’, attended by a crew of gods. At sunset he changes vessels and boards the night-barque to travel through the Duat, the underworld, hour by hour.

The New Kingdom Book of the Hidden Chamber, the Amduat, painted on the walls of royal tombs, maps the twelve hours of that voyage. In the seventh hour the serpent Apep lies across the way, and the boat's defenders bind and cut him with knives while Isis speaks her spells. The sun god in his ram-headed night form calls to the dead along the banks, who wake briefly in his light and lament when he moves on. In the twelfth hour the boat is drawn through the body of a vast serpent, entering at the tail and leaving at the mouth, and the sun emerges as Khepri, the scarab, reborn on the eastern horizon.

Every dawn is a rescue.

image.caption: Ra travels through the underworld in his barque, Book of Gates, tomb of Ramesses I (KV16), c. 1290 BCE

versions.title: Shamash Through the Mountain
versions.teaser: The sun god steps out between the eastern mountains every dawn.
versions.text:
Cylinder seals of the Akkadian period show a favourite scene: Shamash, rays rising from his shoulders, stepping up between two mountains while attendant gods swing open the doors of heaven. In his hand he holds a serrated blade, his emblem as judge. At dusk he enters the western mountain and passes through the interior of the earth, where he is judge of the dead as well, to reappear in the east.

The Epic of Gilgamesh lets a mortal walk that road. Seeking Utnapishtim, Gilgamesh reaches the twin peaks of Mashu, which guard the sun at its rising and setting and are watched by scorpion-people. They let him into the tunnel the sun travels by night. For twelve double-hours he runs in total darkness, unable to see ahead or behind, until the light breaks and he emerges into a garden where the trees bear carnelian and their leaves are lapis lazuli.

It is a road meant for the sun alone, and one desperate king.

image.caption: The Adda Seal: Shamash rising between the mountains, Akkadian, c. 2300 BCE (British Museum)

versions.title: Sūrya and the Seven Mares
versions.teaser: Seven bay mares draw the Vedic sun across the vault of heaven.
versions.text:
In the Rigveda the sun is both a god and a visible thing: Sūrya, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa and Agni, a jewel of the sky. He rides a chariot drawn by seven bay mares, and the hymn to him (Rigveda 1.50) pictures the stars slinking away with the night ‘like thieves’ as the all-seeing god approaches, while his rays run ahead of him over the peoples.

Another hymn (1.115) makes sunset an act of unharnessing: when Sūrya unyokes his mares, Night spreads her garment over everything. One of his forms is endless and bright, the other black. The Vedic poets cared less about the sun's night journey than about its return, and Uṣas, the Dawn, drives her own ruddy team ahead of him.

The image lasted two thousand years. At Konark in Odisha, the thirteenth-century Sun Temple was built as a colossal stone chariot, with twenty-four carved wheels and seven horses to pull it.

image.caption: One of the carved chariot wheels of the Sun Temple at Konark, 13th century

versions.title: Helios and the Golden Cup
versions.teaser: A chariot by day, and a golden vessel round the Ocean by night.
versions.text:
Helios, son of the Titan Hyperion, drives his chariot up out of the eastern Ocean each morning. The Homeric Hymn to Helios describes the light flashing from his golden helmet, and his team resting at the height of heaven before he sends them down again to Ocean in the west. He sees everything, which is why Demeter goes to him to learn who took her daughter.

The return journey is solved by the lyric poets. In Mimnermus the tired sun lies down in a winged golden bed made by Hephaestus, which carries him over the waves while he sleeps, from the land of the Hesperides back to the Ethiopians in the east, where his chariot and horses wait. In Stesichorus it is a golden cup, and Heracles borrows it to sail to the island of Geryon.

The chariot has one famous failure. Ovid's Phaethon, son of the Sun, begs for a single day at the reins, loses control, scorches Libya into desert, and is struck down by Jupiter's thunderbolt.

image.caption: Helios or Phaethon driving the chariot of the Sun, ornamental print after Rosso Fiorentino, 16th century (Metropolitan Museum of Art)

versions.title: Mithra Before the Sun
versions.teaser: The god of the contract climbs the mountain ahead of the swift-horsed sun.
versions.text:
The Avestan hymns separate the sun from its escort. Hvarə Khšaēta, the ‘radiant sun’, has a short hymn of his own (Yasht 6), in which he is called swift-horsed. When he rises, the earth, the flowing waters and the plants are made clean; if he did not rise, the demons would destroy everything in the seven regions of the world.

Mithra, the god of the contract, is not the sun but its forerunner. His great hymn (Yasht 10.13) says he is the first of the spiritual gods to climb over Mount Harā ahead of the immortal, swift-horsed sun, taking hold of the gold-adorned peaks and surveying the lands of the Iranians. Elsewhere in the same hymn Mithra drives his own chariot behind four white horses, shod in front with gold and behind with silver. Guardian of every agreement, he has a thousand ears and ten thousand eyes.

Roman dedications later call Mithras the Unconquered Sun, though how much Roman Mithraism owes to Iran is still debated.

versions.title: The Ten Suns of Fusang
versions.teaser: Ten suns take turns crossing the sky, carried by crows, bathed by their mother.
versions.text:
The Classic of Mountains and Seas describes a valley in the far east, Tanggu, the ‘Hot Water Valley’, where the suns bathe. Over it grows the giant Fusang tree. There are ten suns: nine rest on its lower branches while one sits at the top, and each day one sets out as another comes home, each carried, another passage says, on a crow. Their mother is Xihe, who bathes her children in the Gan Abyss beyond the south-eastern sea.

In the Chuci poems Xihe becomes the sun's charioteer, and the poet of the Lisao, anxious to hold back the evening, orders her to slow her pace. The Huainanzi traces the sun's daily route through named stations, from the valley of its rising to the abyss where it sets.

The system works as long as the suns take turns. When all ten rise together, the earth burns, and the archer Yi must shoot down nine of them.

image.caption: Heaven on the Mawangdui silk banner, with the sun-crow, suns in the Fusang tree and the moon, Han dynasty, 2nd century BCE

versions.title: Sól and the Wolf
versions.teaser: The sun's driver hurries because a wolf is always behind her.
versions.text:
In Snorri's account, a man named Mundilfari had two children so beautiful that he named them Moon and Sun. The gods, angered by his presumption, took them and set them in the sky. Sól drives the horses Árvakr, ‘Early-waker’, and Alsviðr, ‘All-swift’, that pull the sun, and the gods set bellows under the horses' shoulders to cool them. The Eddic poem Grímnismál adds a shield, Svalinn, that stands before the sun; if it fell, mountains and sea would burn.

Sól drives fast because she is hunted. The wolf Sköll runs behind her, and another wolf, Hati, runs ahead after the moon. One day, Snorri says, they will catch them.

A far older image comes from Danish soil: the Trundholm sun chariot, a bronze horse drawing a gilded disc on wheels, made around 1400 BCE. Whatever it meant to its makers, the idea of a horse pulling the sun ran deep in the north.
versions.caveat: The Trundholm chariot is more than two thousand years older than the Norse texts, so any link to Sól is speculative.

image.file: File:Trundholm sun chariot Nationalmuseet.jpg
image.caption: The Trundholm sun chariot, bronze and gold, Denmark, c. 1400 BCE (National Museum of Denmark)

versions.title: Tonatiuh's Escort
versions.teaser: Dead warriors carry the sun up; women who died in childbirth carry it down.
versions.text:
The Aztec sun, Tonatiuh, does not travel alone. According to the accounts Bernardino de Sahagún collected from Nahua elders, warriors who died in battle or on the sacrificial stone went to the house of the sun in the east. Each morning they greeted him with shouts, clashing their shields, and escorted him to the zenith.

At noon they handed him over to the cihuateteo, the women who had died in childbirth, honoured as warriors who had fallen while taking a captive. They carried the sun down to the west in a litter of quetzal feathers, and there he entered the land of the dead. After four years the warrior souls became birds and butterflies, sipping at flowers.

The sun's motion was never guaranteed. In the story of the Fifth Sun, recorded in the same work, the newly created sun hangs motionless in the sky until the gods give their own lives to set it moving. Blood keeps it on its road.

versions.title: Māui Slows the Sun
versions.teaser: A trickster lassoes the sun and beats it into walking slowly.
versions.text:
In Polynesia the sun's problem is not its route but its speed. In the Hawaiian telling, Māui's mother Hina cannot dry her bark cloth because the sun races across the sky too quickly. Māui climbs Haleakalā, the ‘House of the Sun’, braids strong cords, and snares the sun's rays one by one as they come over the crater rim. The sun pleads for its life and agrees to go slowly for half the year.

The Māori version, recorded by George Grey, has Māui and his brothers build walls of clay beside the pit where the sun rises, noose him as he comes up, and beat him with the enchanted jawbone of Māui's ancestress Muri-ranga-whenua. The wounded sun cries out, betraying his secret name, Tama-nui-te-rā, and ever since he has crept slowly along his path.

The long summer day, in other words, is a truce.

concepts.summary: An eclipse is the sky's most frightening irregularity, and many peoples explained it as the sun or moon being eaten, attacked, sickened or stolen. The response was usually loud and practical: drums, shouting, beaten dogs, substitute kings. Babylon and China also recorded eclipses and learned to predict them, without giving up the rituals. The devouring monster turns up on every continent, and is best explained as independent invention prompted by what an eclipse looks like, a bite taken out of a bright disc, rather than by any shared origin.

versions.title: The Seven Against the Moon
versions.teaser: Seven demons besiege the moon god, and the king must hide.
versions.text:
Babylonian scholars kept eclipse records for centuries and learned to forecast lunar eclipses with growing skill, but knowing when did not answer why. An incantation from the series Utukkū Lemnūtu, ‘Evil Spirits’, gives the mythic reason. Seven demons, born in the depths of heaven, rush upon the moon god Sîn and surround him, while the other great lights of the sky fail to stand by him, and Sîn is darkened. Enlil sees his son's distress and sends his vizier to Ea, who dispatches Marduk to drive the demons away.

The practical response was stranger. Because an eclipse could portend the king's death, Neo-Assyrian scholars enthroned a substitute king to take the omen on himself, while the real king kept out of sight and was addressed in letters only as ‘the farmer’. When the danger had passed, the substitute ‘went to his fate’, and the real king returned to his throne.

versions.title: Rāhu's Severed Head
versions.teaser: A demon's immortal head chases the sun and moon forever.
versions.text:
The oldest Indian eclipse is in the Rigveda (5.40): the demon Svarbhānu pierces the sun with darkness, and all creatures stand bewildered until the seer Atri finds the hidden sun and sets it back in the sky.

The story that lasted comes from the Mahābhārata's account of the churning of the ocean. When gods and demons churn the Ocean of Milk for amṛta, the drink of immortality, Viṣṇu takes the form of a bewitching woman to serve it only to the gods. The demon Rāhu slips into their line in disguise and drinks. The Sun and Moon raise the alarm, and Viṣṇu's discus cuts off his head while the amṛta is still in his throat.

The head, now immortal, rises to the sky and keeps its grudge against the two informers. At intervals it swallows the Sun or the Moon. They always reappear, later tellings explain, because a head with no body cannot hold them.
sources: Mahābhārata 1 (Ādiparvan), the churning of the ocean

image.caption: Rahu, the severed demon head, 19th-century Indian illustration published by E. A. Rodrigues

versions.title: The Sun Is Eaten
versions.teaser: Chronicles record the sun ‘eaten’, and drums at the altar of the soil.
versions.text:
Chinese has a blunt word for an eclipse: shi, ‘eating’. The Spring and Autumn Annals, the court chronicle of the state of Lu, record more than thirty solar eclipses with the formula ‘the sun was eaten’, and some entries add what was done about it: drums were beaten and victims offered at the altar of the soil. The Zuozhuan commentary argues over whether these were the correct rites for the occasion, which shows that the response was a matter of ritual propriety as much as panic.

In Han cosmology an eclipse was a portent aimed at the ruler, a sign that yin had overcome yang and that government had gone astray; emperors issued edicts of self-reproach in response. Court astronomers, meanwhile, tried to predict them.

Who does the eating? In later popular belief it is Tiangou, the Heavenly Dog, and villagers would bang pots and gongs to make it spit the sun back out.
versions.caveat: The Heavenly Dog as eclipse-eater is a later folk belief; the classical sources speak only of the sun being ‘eaten’.

versions.title: The Wolf That Catches the Sun
versions.teaser: At the end of the world the wolf finally closes its jaws.
versions.text:
No Norse source explains ordinary eclipses, but several tell how the sun will finally be swallowed. The wolf Sköll has chased Sól across the sky since the beginning, and Hati runs after the moon. Snorri adds that in the Iron Wood east of Midgard an old giantess breeds wolves, and that the mightiest of her brood, Mánagarmr, ‘Moon-hound’, will gorge on the lifeblood of everyone who dies, swallow the moon, and spatter the heavens with blood, so that the sun loses its shine.

At Ragnarök the pursuit ends. Völuspá sees the sun turn black, the earth sink into the sea, and the bright stars fall from heaven.

Yet Vafþrúðnismál holds out a kind of remedy. Before the wolf Fenrir overtakes her, the sun will bear a daughter no less beautiful than herself, and when the gods are dead the girl will ride her mother's road.
versions.caveat: These are end-of-the-world swallowings; no surviving Norse text uses the wolves to explain ordinary eclipses.

image.caption: The Wolves Pursuing Sol and Mani, J. C. Dollman, 1909

versions.title: When the Tzitzimime Descend
versions.teaser: If the sun were wholly eaten, the star-demons would come down.
versions.text:
Sahagún's Nahua informants described a solar eclipse as the sun being eaten. When it happened there was uproar. People cried out; men raised the warbling war-cry, striking their mouths with their hands. Captives were sacrificed, and men of fair complexion were sought out and slain, their blood offered to the darkened sun.

The fear was specific. If the eclipse were completed, it was said, darkness would last forever, and the tzitzimime, star-demons waiting in the sky, would come down to eat humankind. An eclipse of the moon carried its own danger: pregnant women feared that the child would be born with a split lip, or turned into a mouse, and they protected the unborn by placing a flake of obsidian in the mouth or at the belly.

The same dread hung over the New Fire ceremony every fifty-two years, when the whole world waited on a mountaintop to see whether the sun would rise again.

versions.title: The Moon's Sickness
versions.teaser: The moon is fainting, and the dogs are beaten to wake her.
versions.text:
The mestizo historian Garcilaso de la Vega, son of an Inca princess, recorded what his mother's people did when the moon was eclipsed. They said the moon was sick, and feared that if she died she would fall from the sky, crush them all, and the world would end. So as the darkness spread they blew trumpets and horns, beat drums and shouted. They tied up their dogs and beat them to make them howl, because the moon was fond of dogs and would take pity on their cries and wake from her fainting. Children were made to weep and call out to Mama Quilla, Mother Moon, begging her not to die.

When the moon recovered, they rejoiced that she had been healed. A solar eclipse, by contrast, meant that the Sun was angry at some offence, his face darkened in wrath as a man's is.

Garcilaso treats it all as pagan error, but a vivid one.
sources: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas (1609), Book 2
versions.caveat: Garcilaso wrote in Spain decades after the conquest, from memory and for a Spanish readership.

versions.title: Louhi Steals the Sun
versions.teaser: The mistress of the north locks the sun and moon inside a mountain.
versions.text:
In the Kalevala, darkness comes by theft. After the heroes carry off the Sampo, Louhi, mistress of the northern land of Pohjola, takes her revenge. The sun and moon have come down to sit in the treetops and listen to Väinämöinen playing his new kantele; Louhi seizes them and shuts them inside a rocky mountain, and steals the fire from the hearths of Kalevala as well. Darkness settles over the land, and even Ukko, the sky god, wanders the edges of the clouds wondering where the light has gone.

The smith Ilmarinen tries to forge a new moon of gold and a new sun of silver and hangs them high in the trees, but they will not shine. At last he sets about forging a collar and fetters for Louhi. Frightened, she lets the sun and moon go, and Väinämöinen greets them as they rise.
versions.caveat: The Kalevala is Elias Lönnrot's 1849 compilation from folk songs, and this is a theft of the sun rather than an explanation of eclipses.

versions.title: The Great Frog
versions.teaser: A great frog tries to swallow the sun; drums and gunfire drive it off.
versions.text:
James Mooney, who worked among the Eastern Cherokee in the late 1880s, recorded a short, precise explanation. When the sun or moon is eclipsed, it is because a great frog in the sky is trying to swallow it. Everybody knew this, his informants said, the Creeks and other peoples too. In the old days, before the great medicine men had all died, the people would come together whenever they saw the sun grow dark, fire guns and beat the drum, and in a little while the frog would be frightened off and the sun would be well again.

The Cherokee sun is also a person. In another story Mooney collected, she is a woman whose daughter is killed by a snake sent against the Sun herself. Grieving, she shuts herself away and the world goes dark, until the people bring drummers and singers to play before her, and at last she lifts her face and smiles.
sources: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900)

concepts.summary: The moon has a face, or a figure, and people have always wanted to know whose. Traditions from India to Japan see a hare, an image spread partly by Buddhist storytelling; China adds an exiled woman, a toad and a woodcutter; Mesoamerica sees a rabbit too, independently. Elsewhere the dwellers are children snatched while fetching water, a woman carried off with her gourd, a brother marked with soot, or the souls of the dead. The markings are the same everywhere, but what they resemble depends on what a culture already expected to see.

versions.title: The Hare's Sacrifice
versions.teaser: A hare leaps into the fire and is drawn on the moon forever.
versions.text:
In the Sasa Jātaka, one of the stories of the Buddha's former lives, the Bodhisatta is born as a hare who lives with three friends, a monkey, a jackal and an otter. The others each find some food to offer; the hare, who eats only grass, has nothing a human could eat, and resolves to give his own body.

Sakka, king of the gods, comes disguised as a hungry brahmin to test him. The hare tells him to light a fire, shakes himself three times so that no creature living in his fur will be burned, and leaps into the flames. The fire feels as cool as frost. Sakka reveals himself and, so that the hare's virtue will be known for an entire aeon, squeezes a mountain and with its essence draws the hare's outline on the face of the moon.

In Sanskrit the moon is śaśin, ‘the one with the hare’.

versions.title: Chang'e, the Toad and the Hare
versions.teaser: A woman who stole immortality lives on in a crowded moon.
versions.text:
The Huainanzi, compiled in the second century BCE, gives the terse original: the archer Yi obtained the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West, and his wife Heng'e stole it and fled to the moon. Her name was later changed to Chang'e to avoid the personal name of a Han emperor. Other early writers say she became a toad there, and Han tomb art puts a toad and a hare side by side in the lunar disc, the hare often pounding the elixir with mortar and pestle.

The Tang writer Duan Chengshi adds a fourth resident. A man named Wu Gang, who committed a fault while studying immortality, is condemned to chop down the cassia tree on the moon, but every cut closes up as soon as the axe comes out. He is still at it.

At the Mid-Autumn Festival, families look up at a crowded moon: a lonely woman, her hare, a toad and a woodcutter.

image.caption: The crescent moon with its toad, detail of the Mawangdui silk banner, Han dynasty, 2nd century BCE

versions.title: The Souls on the Moon
versions.teaser: Plutarch fills the moon's hollows with the souls of the dead.
versions.text:
Greek poetry has a moon goddess, Selene, who drives her team across the night and falls in love with the sleeping Endymion. But the most searching Greek account of who lives in the moon is a philosophical dialogue. In Plutarch's On the Face Which Appears in the Orb of the Moon, the speakers argue about the markings: are they a reflection of the ocean, an optical effect, or real shadows on an earthy body with mountains and ravines?

The dialogue ends with a myth. After death, souls rise into the region between earth and moon, where the unjust are punished and the good are purified. The worthy then come to dwell on the moon itself as daimones, who descend to earth at times to watch over oracles and mysteries. The moon's great hollows are named places; the largest is the Recess of Hecate, where souls suffer and pay penalties.

In a second death, the mind parts from the soul on the moon and goes on to the sun.
sources: Plutarch, De facie in orbe lunae (On the Face in the Moon)

versions.title: Bil and Hjúki
versions.teaser: Two children with a bucket, snatched up by the Moon.
versions.text:
Snorri's Gylfaginning says that Máni, the Moon, steers the moon's course and governs its waxing and waning, and that he once took two children up from the earth. They were Bil and Hjúki, children of a man named Viðfinnr, and at the moment of capture they were walking from the well called Byrgir, carrying between them on their shoulders the pail Sægr on the pole Simul. They follow Máni still, Snorri says, as can be seen from the earth.

That is all the source gives, but it is enough for a picture: two small figures with a bucket on a yoke, visible in the moon's spots. Nineteenth-century writers eagerly connected them with the English nursery rhyme of Jack and Jill, who went up the hill to fetch a pail of water.
versions.caveat: The Jack and Jill connection is nineteenth-century speculation with no evidence behind it.

image.caption: Máni and Sól, Lorenz Frølich, 1895

versions.title: The Princess from the Moon
versions.teaser: A girl found in a bamboo stalk turns out to be a moon exile.
versions.text:
The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, the oldest surviving Japanese prose tale, opens with an old man who finds a tiny girl, three inches tall, glowing inside a stalk of bamboo. In three months she grows into a woman of unearthly beauty, Kaguya-hime. Five noble suitors are set impossible tasks, such as fetching the Buddha's stone begging bowl or the jewel from a dragon's neck, and each fails or cheats. Even the emperor cannot win her.

At last she confesses that she is one of the people of the moon, sent down to earth for a fault. On the night of the full moon a host descends on a cloud, and the emperor's soldiers find their arms go limp. A robe of feathers is put on her, and with it she forgets all earthly sorrow. She leaves the emperor an elixir of immortality, which he orders burned on the mountain nearest heaven.

Its smoke, they say, still rises from Fuji.
sources: Taketori monogatari (The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter), 9th–10th c.

image.file: File:Taketori Monogatari 2.jpg
image.caption: Princess Kaguya returns to the moon, painting by Tosa Hiromichi and Tosa Hirosumi, 17th century

versions.title: The Rabbit in the Moon's Face
versions.teaser: The gods dim the second sun by throwing a rabbit at it.
versions.text:
The Nahua account of how the present sun and moon were made, recorded by Sahagún, explains the moon's markings with a blow. In the darkness at Teotihuacan the gods ask who will light the world. The proud, rich Tecuciztecatl volunteers; the poor, pock-marked Nanahuatzin is chosen as well. Before the divine hearth Tecuciztecatl flinches from the flames four times. Nanahuatzin leaps at once and burns, and only then does Tecuciztecatl follow.

Nanahuatzin rises as the sun. Tecuciztecatl rises after him, shining just as brightly, and the gods, unwilling to have two equal lights, send one of their number running to strike him in the face with a rabbit. That dimmed his face, and the rabbit's shape is still there.

Classic Maya art shows the moon goddess cradling a rabbit, so the image was at home in Mesoamerica long before Sahagún wrote it down.

versions.title: The Moon Brother
versions.teaser: A brother and sister run into the sky, one as sun, one as moon.
versions.text:
Across the Arctic, Inuit tell of a brother and sister who became the moon and the sun. In versions recorded by Hinrich Rink in Greenland and Franz Boas on Baffin Island, a girl is visited in the dark, night after night, by a lover whose face she cannot see. To find him out she blackens her hands with soot from the lamp and marks him, and in the light she sees the smudges on her own brother. Horrified, she seizes a burning torch and runs; he snatches up another and chases her. As they run they rise into the sky. She becomes the sun, carrying the bright flame. His torch dwindles to embers, and he becomes the moon.

The dark patches on the moon are the soot on his face. He still pursues her, and in many regions the moon man has a house in the sky and a dog team, and comes down to hunt or to see that taboos are kept.
sources: Hinrich Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875)

versions.title: Rona and the Moon
versions.teaser: A woman curses the moon and is carried off, tree and all.
versions.text:
Rona goes out one night to fetch water from a stream, carrying a gourd. The path is moonlit, but then the moon slips behind a cloud and she stumbles over roots in the dark. In her anger she curses the moon, calling it a cooked head, the worst of insults. The moon hears, comes down and seizes her. Rona clutches at a ngaio tree, but the moon pulls it up by the roots and carries off woman, gourd and tree together.

She is there still: the dark patches on the moon are Rona with her calabash and her tree, a warning to anyone who curses what gives them light.

Hawaiians see a different woman in the moon: Hina, who climbed up there with her gourd to escape the endless labour of earth, and who still beats out her bark cloth among the clouds.

concepts.summary: Knowledge in myth is rarely free. The wise pay with an eye, with innocence, with a head, with years of patience, with pursuit through many shapes, or with their place in paradise; sometimes someone else pays, tricked out of a secret he meant to keep. The pattern reflects a widespread intuition that knowledge is power taken from the gods or the world, and that power has costs. The burned-thumb stories of Ireland and Wales are clearly related to each other; most of the rest are independent reflections on the same bargain.

versions.title: Enkidu Becomes Wise
versions.teaser: The wild man gains understanding and loses the gazelles.
versions.text:
Enkidu is made from clay in the wilderness, a hairy man who grazes with gazelles and drinks at the waterholes with the beasts. To tame him, a trapper brings Shamhat, a woman of the temple, and for six days and seven nights Enkidu lies with her.

When he rises and goes back to his herd, the gazelles see him and run. His body has been drained; his legs, which used to keep pace with the animals, stand still. But, the poem says, he now has reason and broad understanding. Shamhat tells him that he has become like a god, and leads him to bread, beer, clothes, and the city of Uruk.

Later, dying, Enkidu curses Shamhat for taking him from the wild, and Shamash rebukes him: she fed you bread fit for a god and gave you Gilgamesh for a friend. Enkidu relents and blesses her. The price of being human has been paid, and on reflection he thinks it fair.
sources: Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablets I, II and VII

versions.title: Dadhyañc's Horse Head
versions.teaser: A sage keeps his promise to Indra by teaching through a horse's mouth.
versions.text:
The sage Dadhyañc knows the madhu-vidyā, the secret doctrine of the ‘honey’, and Indra has taught it to him on one condition: if he ever passes it on, Indra will cut off his head. The twin gods of healing, the Aśvins, want the knowledge badly, and they have a plan. They cut off the sage's head themselves, set it aside, and fit him with the head of a horse. Through the horse's mouth he teaches them the honey-doctrine.

Indra, true to his word, strikes off the horse's head. The Aśvins then put back the sage's own, and he is none the worse. The Rigveda alludes to the story twice as a famous exploit of the twins, and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa tells it in full.

The lesson is thoroughly Vedic: a secret can be kept to the letter and given away all the same.

versions.title: Isis and the Secret Name
versions.teaser: Isis poisons the sun god to learn the one name she lacks.
versions.text:
Ra has grown old; his mouth trembles and his spittle drips to the ground. Isis, who knows everything in heaven and earth except the sun god's secret name, gathers the spittle, kneads it with earth into a serpent, and leaves it on the path where Ra walks each day.

The snake bites him. The god who created all things is burned by a poison he did not make and does not know, and his limbs shake. The gods gather around him lamenting, and Isis comes too, offering to cure him if he will tell her his name. Ra recites his titles: I am Khepri in the morning, Ra at noon, Atum in the evening. The poison does not budge. At last, in agony, he lets his hidden name pass from his body into hers, and she speaks the spell that draws out the venom.

The tale is itself a charm: it was recited over people stung by scorpions or bitten by snakes.

versions.title: The Tree of Knowledge
versions.teaser: Eyes opened, and the garden gate closed behind them.
versions.text:
In the garden in Eden grow two special trees: the tree of life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The man may eat from any tree but the second, ‘for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die’. The serpent, more cunning than any beast of the field, tells the woman otherwise: she will not die, but her eyes will be opened, and she will be like God, knowing good and evil.

In a sense both are right. The couple eat, their eyes are opened, and the first thing they know is that they are naked. They do not die that day. But God, observing that the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil, sends them out of the garden before they can reach for the tree of life as well, and sets cherubim and a flaming, turning sword at its gate.

Knowledge was theirs to keep. Immortality was the price.

image.caption: The Fall of Man, Lucas Cranach the Elder, 16th century

versions.title: The Blinding of Tiresias
versions.teaser: Two stories, one exchange: eyesight for foresight.
versions.text:
Greek myth gives two stories of how the prophet Tiresias lost his sight, and in both prophecy is the compensation. In one, which Apollodorus attributes to Hesiod and Ovid also tells, Tiresias strikes two mating snakes and is turned into a woman; years later he does it again and becomes a man. Zeus and Hera, arguing whether men or women take more pleasure in love, ask the one person who knows. Tiresias says that of ten parts, the woman enjoys nine. Hera blinds him for it; Zeus, unable to undo another god's act, gives him prophecy and a life of seven generations.

In the other, told by Callimachus, the young Tiresias stumbles on Athena bathing. She cannot undo the law that such a sight costs the eyes, but in pity she grants him understanding of the birds and a long life.

Either way, Greek prophecy begins where eyesight ends.

image.caption: Tiresias transformed into a woman, Pietro della Vecchia, 17th century

versions.title: When Cangjie Made Writing
versions.teaser: Writing is invented; Heaven rains millet and ghosts weep.
versions.text:
Cangjie, the legendary scribe of the Yellow Emperor, is said to have devised the first Chinese characters by studying the tracks of birds and beasts. The invention was not greeted calmly. The Huainanzi records what happened in a single line: in antiquity, when Cangjie created writing, Heaven rained millet and ghosts wailed in the night.

The Han commentator Gao You explained the omens. Once people could write, deceit would sprout; they would abandon farming for the profits of the clerk's knife and brush, and Heaven, foreseeing the famine, sent grain down in advance. The ghosts wailed because they feared being indicted by written documents.

The line sits in a chapter lamenting how each new human cleverness has carried people further from the original simplicity of the Way. Writing was a triumph, and Heaven wept grain over it.
sources: Gao You's commentary on the Huainanzi

versions.title: Odin's Eye and the Tree
versions.teaser: An eye in the well, nine nights on the tree, and then the runes.
versions.text:
Odin, the wisest of the gods, bought his wisdom in instalments. The seeress of Völuspá knows where his eye is: pledged in Mímir's well beneath a root of Yggdrasil, where Mímir drinks mead every morning from the god's pledge. Snorri explains that Odin was refused a single drink from the well, whose water holds wisdom and understanding, until he gave up the eye.

In Hávamál, Odin himself describes a harder bargain. He hung on the windswept tree, whose roots no one knows, nine full nights, wounded with a spear, given to Odin, himself to himself. No one gave him bread or drink. He peered down, took up the runes screaming, and fell back. Then he began to grow, and to be wise.

The mead of poetry, which he won by seducing the giantess Gunnlöð and escaping in eagle form, cost him far less, but only because someone else paid.

image.caption: Odin drinking at the well of wisdom, Robert Engels, early 20th century

versions.title: Fionn and the Salmon
versions.teaser: Seven years of waiting, and a boy burns his thumb.
versions.text:
The poet Finnéces has spent seven years beside a pool on the river Boyne, watching for the salmon of Féc's Pool, for it was prophesied that a man named Finn would eat it and nothing would be unknown to him. When at last he catches it, he gives it to his young pupil, Demne, to cook, with strict orders not to eat any.

The boy brings it cooked. Has he eaten any of it? No, says the boy, but I burned my thumb on it and put it in my mouth. Finnéces asks his name. Demne, he says. Your name is Finn, says the poet, and it was to you the salmon was given in prophecy: eat it. From then on, whenever Fionn puts his thumb in his mouth, what he did not know is revealed to him.

The cost falls on Finnéces, whose seven years of patience go to a boy with a sore thumb, and he gives them up with good grace.
sources: Macgnímartha Finn (The Boyhood Deeds of Fionn)

versions.title: Gwion and the Cauldron
versions.teaser: Three drops of wisdom, and a chase through every shape.
versions.text:
The enchantress Ceridwen, grieving that her son Morfran is the ugliest boy alive, resolves to make up for his looks with wisdom. She sets a cauldron boiling for a year and a day, adding herbs gathered at the proper hours, and puts a boy, Gwion Bach, to stir it. At the end of the year three drops of the brew leap out onto Gwion's thumb; he puts it in his mouth and at once knows everything, including that Ceridwen will kill him. The rest of the cauldron, now poison, cracks apart.

Gwion runs. He becomes a hare and she a greyhound; he a fish and she an otter; he a bird and she a hawk; at last he becomes a grain of wheat on a threshing floor, and she a black hen who swallows him. Nine months later she bears him, too beautiful to kill, and sets him adrift in a leather bag. He is found and named Taliesin, ‘radiant brow’, the greatest of poets.
sources: Hanes Taliesin (in Elis Gruffydd's chronicle, 16th c.)
versions.caveat: The full tale survives only in sixteenth-century versions, though the poet Taliesin and the poems attributed to him are much older.

versions.title: Into the Belly of Vipunen
versions.teaser: The old sage goes inside a dead giant to fetch three words.
versions.text:
Väinämöinen is building a boat by singing, but he lacks three words to finish it. He looks for them in the heads of swallows and swans, and under the tongue of a reindeer, and finds nothing. A shepherd tells him where the old words are: in the mouth of Antero Vipunen, a long-dead giant sage who lies under the earth, with an aspen growing from his shoulders and a birch from his temples.

The smith Ilmarinen forges him iron shoes and gloves, and Väinämöinen goes, pries open the giant's jaw, and tumbles in. Vipunen swallows him. Inside, Väinämöinen sets up a forge, his shirt for bellows and his knee for an anvil, and hammers at the giant's innards until Vipunen, in torment, opens the chest of his songs. He sings for days, and Väinämöinen comes out with the words he needed, and many more.

In Finnic lore, knowledge must be fetched from the dead, at some cost to the fetcher.
versions.caveat: The Kalevala is Elias Lönnrot's nineteenth-century compilation, though the Vipunen songs were widely collected in Karelia.

concepts.summary: From Anatolia to Scandinavia, fate is something spun, measured or woven, usually by women and often at the moment of birth. The metaphor comes naturally to societies in which spinning and weaving were women's constant work, and it may also be an old inheritance among Indo-European speakers, from the Hittites to the Norse. Egypt has birth-fate goddesses who pronounce rather than spin, and Tang China binds future spouses with an invisible red cord. The idea is the same everywhere: a life has a length and a pattern, fixed before its owner has any say.

versions.title: The Spinners of the King's Years
versions.teaser: Two underworld goddesses kneel with a spindle and spin the king's years.
versions.text:
In a Hittite ritual for the founding of a new palace, the king is shown two old goddesses of the underworld, Išduštaya and Papaya, kneeling at their work. One holds a spindle, the other what seems to be a mirror, and they are spinning the king's years. The text promises that those years will have no end and no number, and the ritual asks the goddesses to keep the thread running.

Beside them the Hittites honoured the Gulšeš, whose name probably comes from a verb meaning ‘to engrave’ or ‘to write’: goddesses of destiny who allotted each person's life and received offerings at festivals. The metaphor shifts from thread to inscription, but the idea is the same.

These texts, from the royal archives of Hattusa in the second millennium BCE, are among the oldest anywhere to picture fate as spinning, centuries before Homer.
sources: Hittite ritual for the foundation of a palace (CTH 414)

versions.title: The Seven Hathors
versions.teaser: At each birth, seven goddesses announce how the child will die.
versions.text:
Egyptian fate is spoken, not spun. When a child is born, the Seven Hathors come to decree its destiny. In the New Kingdom Tale of the Doomed Prince, a long-awaited son is born to a king, and the Hathors pronounce: he will die by the crocodile, the snake or the dog. The king builds him a stone house in the desert, but the boy sees a dog from the roof and insists on having one, and the story becomes a tale of fates dodged one by one. The papyrus breaks off before the end.

The Tale of Two Brothers uses the same device. When the gods fashion a wife for Bata, the Seven Hathors come to see her and say with one voice that she will die by the knife.

Behind them stand Shai, whose name means ‘what is ordained’, and Renenutet, who grants each person an allotted portion.
sources: Tale of the Doomed Prince (Papyrus Harris 500)

versions.title: Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos
versions.teaser: The Spinner, the Allotter and the Unturnable sit at Necessity's spindle.
versions.text:
Homer speaks of fate as thread already spun. Hecuba, mourning Hector, says it was his lot from the day he was born, what mighty Fate spun for him with her thread, to glut the dogs far from his parents. In the Odyssey, King Alcinous speaks of the ‘heavy Spinners’ who spin a man's portion at his birth.

Hesiod names three Moirai: Clotho, the Spinner; Lachesis, the Allotter; and Atropos, the Unturnable. The Theogony, rather awkwardly, makes them daughters of Night in one passage and of Zeus and Themis in another.

Plato gives them their grandest setting. In the Myth of Er, at the end of the Republic, they sit around the spindle of Necessity, whose whorls carry the circles of the planets. Lachesis sings of what has been, Clotho of what is, Atropos of what will be. Each soul choosing its next life receives a guardian spirit from Lachesis, and passes under Clotho's hand and Atropos's spinning, so that its choice can never be undone.

versions.title: The Old Man Under the Moon
versions.teaser: A red cord, tied at birth, binds husband and wife.
versions.text:
A Tang tale in Li Fuyan's collection Xu Xuanguai lu tells of Wei Gu, a young man anxious to marry, who comes upon an old man at dawn, reading a book by moonlight on the steps of a temple. The book, the old man explains, is the register of marriages kept in the other world, and in his bag he carries red cords with which he secretly ties together the feet of those destined to wed. Once tied, nothing parts them, not feud, not distance.

Wei Gu's destined wife, he learns, is a three-year-old girl, daughter of a poor woman who sells vegetables in the market. Appalled, he sends a servant to kill the child; the man only wounds her between the eyebrows. Fourteen years later Wei Gu marries a beautiful girl who always wears an ornament on her brow. She is, of course, the same child.

The old man, Yue Lao, became the god of marriage, and the red thread of destiny a byword across East Asia.
sources: Li Fuyan, Xu Xuanguai lu, ‘The Inn of Betrothal’ (9th c.)

versions.title: The Norns at the Well
versions.teaser: Three women at the world-tree's root cut staves and choose lives.
versions.text:
At the foot of Yggdrasil, by the well of Urðr, live three maidens, Völuspá says: Urðr, Verðandi and Skuld. They cut staves, lay down laws and choose lives for the children of men. Their names are usually glossed ‘what came to be’, ‘what is coming to be’ and ‘what shall be’, though Skuld may rather mean ‘debt’. Snorri adds that they water the tree each day from the well to keep it from rotting.

The first poem of Helgi shows norns at work. On the night of the hero's birth they come to his father's hall, twist the strands of his fate, and stretch out the golden cord, fastening it beneath the moon's hall and hiding its ends in the east and west.

In Njáls saga, a man in Caithness looks through a window and sees women weaving on a loom whose weights are human heads and whose threads are entrails, chanting the Darraðarljóð. They are weaving the battle of Clontarf.

image.caption: The Norns Urðr, Verðandi and Skuld beneath Yggdrasil, Ludwig Burger, 1882

versions.title: The Sudičky at the Cradle
versions.teaser: Three white women come by night to decide a newborn's fate.
versions.text:
In Czech folk belief, three women, the sudičky, visit a house on one of the first nights after a child's birth to settle its fate. They are usually white-robed and seen, if at all, only by the mother, and each speaks in turn at the cradle: one may grant the child's fortune, another fix the length of its life, the third the manner of its death. South Slavs told of the same visitors as suđaje or rođenice, and Slovenes as rojenice.

Their word cannot be escaped, and folk tales are built on the attempt. In Karel Jaromír Erben's tale of the Three Golden Hairs of Grandfather All-Knowing, a king sheltering in a charcoal-burner's hut overhears the sudičky promise the newborn boy that he will marry the king's own daughter. The king does everything in his power to prevent it, and in doing so brings it about.
sources: Karel Jaromír Erben, ‘Tři zlaté vlasy děda Vševěda’ (1865)
Czech and South Slavic folk belief, recorded in the 19th century
versions.caveat: These are nineteenth-century folk records; their link to the rozhanitsy named in medieval East Slavic sermons, and to any pre-Christian cult, is uncertain.

concepts.summary: The ‘dying and rising god’ is a category built by James Frazer in The Golden Bough, which grouped Tammuz, Adonis, Attis, Osiris and others as vegetation spirits who die and revive with the crops. Jonathan Z. Smith argued that the category collapses under scrutiny: most of these gods die and stay dead, or rule the underworld, and the ‘rising’ is often late or Christian-influenced. Tryggve Mettinger's partial defence held that a few Near Eastern cases, notably Dumuzi and Baal, do involve a real return. The pages below keep each story together with its caveat.

versions.title: Dumuzi Hunted
versions.teaser: The shepherd god dreams his death, runs, and is caught.
versions.text:
In the Sumerian poem Dumuzi's Dream, the shepherd god wakes in terror from a nightmare: rushes rising against him, his churn lying on its side, his drinking cup torn from its peg. His sister Geshtinanna, skilled in dreams, tells him what it means. He is going to die.

The galla, demons of the underworld who take no gifts and know neither wife nor child, come for him. Dumuzi flees and prays to the sun god Utu, his brother-in-law, who turns his hands and feet into a gazelle's so he can escape. Three times he is changed and runs; three times he is caught. Geshtinanna will not betray him, even when the demons torment her, but a friend does. At last the demons find him in his sister's sheepfold. The churn lies silent, the cup is broken, the fold is given to the wind.

His mourning outlived Sumer. Centuries later the prophet Ezekiel saw women at the gate of the Jerusalem temple weeping for Tammuz.
versions.caveat: This poem ends in death; Dumuzi's partial return appears only in the ending of Inanna's Descent, the case Mettinger defends.

versions.title: Osiris Reassembled
versions.teaser: The murdered king is made whole again, but only to rule the dead.
versions.text:
Osiris is murdered by his brother Seth. The Pyramid Texts already know the essentials: Seth struck him down on the riverbank at Nedyt, and Isis and Nephthys searched for him, wailing like kites. Plutarch, writing much later in Greek, gives the full story. Seth tricks Osiris into a chest made to his measure, seals it and throws it into the Nile; Isis finds it at Byblos; Seth finds it again and tears the body into fourteen pieces, which Isis gathers from across Egypt. Only the phallus is lost, eaten by fish.

Isis restores the body, fans breath into it with her wings, and conceives Horus by the revived god. But Osiris does not come back to the world of the living. He becomes ruler of the Duat and judge of the dead, while Horus avenges him on earth.

His revival was real enough to Egyptians, who hoped to become an Osiris themselves at death. It simply led downward.
sources: Great Hymn to Osiris (stela of Amenmose)
versions.caveat: Smith's central example: Osiris revives only as king of the dead, not as a god who returns to life on earth.

image.file: File:Pendentif au nom du roi Osorkon II (Louvre, E 6204).jpg
image.caption: Osiris between Horus and Isis, gold and lapis pendant of Osorkon II, c. 850 BCE (Louvre)

versions.title: Baal and Mot
versions.teaser: The storm god goes down Death's throat, and the rains come back.
versions.text:
In the Baal Cycle from Ugarit, the storm god Baal, newly installed in his palace, defies Mot, whose name means ‘Death’. Mot's answer is his own mouth: one lip to the earth, one to the heavens, a tongue to the stars. Baal must go down into his gullet. He takes with him his clouds, his winds and his rains, and lies with a heifer before he goes. Messengers bring the news to El: mightiest Baal is dead, the Prince, Lord of the Earth, has perished.

Baal's sister Anat searches the land for him and buries his body. Then she seizes Mot, splits him with a blade, winnows him, burns him, grinds him, and sows him in the field for the birds to eat.

Now El dreams: the heavens rain oil, the wadis run with honey. He knows that Baal is alive. In the seventh year Baal and Mot fight again, until the sun goddess Shapash warns Mot, and Death gives way.
versions.caveat: Mettinger's strongest case; even so the tablets are damaged at key points, and whether the story tracks the agricultural year is debated.

image.file: File:Baal thunderbolt Louvre AO15775.jpg
image.caption: Baal with the thunderbolt, limestone stele from Ugarit, 15th–13th century BCE (Louvre)

versions.title: Adonis Divided
versions.teaser: Two goddesses share a beautiful boy, and a boar ends the arrangement.
versions.text:
Adonis is born from a myrrh tree, into which his mother Myrrha was turned. Aphrodite, dazzled by the baby, hides him in a chest and gives it to Persephone to keep; Persephone opens it and refuses to give him back. Zeus, as Apollodorus tells it, divides the year into three: a third Adonis spends with Persephone, a third with Aphrodite, and a third wherever he likes, which he gives to Aphrodite too. Out hunting, he is killed by a boar, and from his blood, in Ovid, springs the short-lived anemone.

His cult is far better attested than his return. At the Athenian Adonia, women planted quick-sprouting seeds in shallow pots on the rooftops, the ‘gardens of Adonis’, let them wither in the summer heat, and mourned. Only the second-century writer Lucian, describing the rites at Byblos, says that after the mourning the worshippers declared Adonis alive and sent him up into the sky.
versions.caveat: The ‘rising’ is attested only late (Lucian and Christian writers); the classical evidence is for mourning, which is why Smith doubted the whole category.

image.file: File:Sebastiano del Piombo - Death of Adonis - WGA21103.jpg
image.caption: The Death of Adonis, Sebastiano del Piombo, c. 1512 (Uffizi)

versions.title: The Death of Baldr
versions.teaser: The whole world weeps for Baldr, except one giantess.
versions.text:
Baldr the Good dreams of his own death, and his mother Frigg takes an oath from fire and water, iron and stone, beasts, birds and poisons, not to harm him; only the mistletoe she thinks too young to ask. The gods make a game of throwing things at him. Loki, disguised, puts a sprig of mistletoe into the hand of Baldr's blind brother Höðr and guides his aim, and Baldr falls dead.

Hermóðr rides nine nights to Hel to ask for his return. Hel agrees on one condition: that everything in the world, living and dead, weep for him. Everything does, even stones and metals, as they do when they come out of frost into warmth, except one giantess in a cave, Þökk, who says she has no use for him. Baldr stays below.

He does come back, but only after the world ends. In Völuspá, when the earth rises green from the sea after Ragnarök, Baldr and Höðr return, reconciled, to live in Odin's hall.
versions.caveat: Baldr's return is a single event after Ragnarök, not a seasonal one; Frazer's vegetation reading of him has little support in the sources.

image.file: File:Each arrow overshot his head by Elmer Boyd Smith.jpg
image.caption: ‘Each arrow overshot his head’: the gods test Baldr, Elmer Boyd Smith, 1902

versions.title: The Maize God Reborn
versions.teaser: A skull in a tree, a miraculous birth, a god rising from a turtle.
versions.text:
In the Popol Vuh, the K'iche' Maya book written down in the sixteenth century, the brothers One Hunahpu and Seven Hunahpu are summoned to Xibalba by the lords of death, fail their tests, and are sacrificed. One Hunahpu's head is hung in a calabash tree, which at once bursts into fruit. When Blood Moon, a daughter of the underworld, reaches toward it, the skull spits into her palm, and she conceives the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

The Twins later defeat the lords of Xibalba and try to restore Seven Hunahpu at the place of his sacrifice. But he can name only a few parts of his face, and he stays there, honoured and prayed to, but not alive.

Classic Maya painted pottery, some eight centuries older, seems to tell a fuller story: a young maize god, attended by the Twins, rising out of a cracked turtle shell that stands for the earth, like a new ear of corn.
sources: Classic Maya painted ceramics (e.g. the ‘Resurrection Plate’, K1892)
versions.caveat: The Classic resurrection is reconstructed from imagery; its link to the Popol Vuh story is widely accepted but interpretive, and the Popol Vuh fathers themselves are not restored to life.

concepts.summary: In this pattern a god does not die but withdraws, in anger, grief or fear, and the world sickens in the god's absence: crops fail, animals stop breeding, the sky goes dark, the gods go hungry or grow old. The story then turns on finding the missing deity and coaxing or tricking them back. The Hittite Telipinu myth gives the pattern its classic form, and it was recited in rituals meant to set real troubles right. The Greek and Japanese versions are almost certainly independent: any farming people knows what the loss of an unseen provider would feel like.

versions.title: When Ishtar Is Gone
versions.teaser: The goddess of love goes below, and desire stops on earth.
versions.text:
In the Akkadian poem of her descent, Ishtar resolves to visit the land of no return, ruled by her sister Ereshkigal. At each of seven gates the gatekeeper strips her of something, her crown, her earrings, her necklaces, the ornaments of her breast, her girdle, her bangles, and at last her garment, until she stands naked before the queen of the dead, who has sixty diseases loosed against her and holds her captive.

Above, the effect is immediate. The bull no longer mounts the cow, the donkey no longer covers the jenny, the young man no longer lies with the girl in the street; he sleeps in his own room, she sleeps on her side.

Ea's remedy is a trick. He creates a handsome courtier, Asushunamir, to charm Ereshkigal into swearing by the great gods, and then to ask for the waterskin. Ishtar is sprinkled with the water of life and led back up through the gates.
sources: Descent of Ishtar to the Netherworld (Akkadian)

image.file: File:Ishtar descent to the Underworld BM ME K.162.jpg
image.caption: Tablet of the Descent of Ishtar from the library of Ashurbanipal, Nineveh, 7th century BCE (British Museum)

versions.title: The Wrath of Telipinu
versions.teaser: A sulking god puts his shoes on the wrong feet, and the land starves.
versions.text:
Telipinu, a god of farming and growth, flies into a rage. He puts his right shoe on his left foot and his left shoe on his right, and storms off. Mist seizes the windows, smoke fills the house; the sheep in the fold and the cows in the pen reject their young. Barley and wheat no longer ripen. Springs and meadows dry up, and gods and humans alike begin to starve.

An eagle searches the mountains and valleys, and the Storm god hammers at Telipinu's gate, but no one finds him. At last the mother goddess Hannahanna sends a little bee. It finds Telipinu asleep in a meadow near the town of Lihzina, stings his hands and feet, and wakes him, which makes him angrier than ever.

The goddess Kamrusepa soothes him with rites of fire, and his rage is sealed in bronze jars in the Dark Earth. Telipinu comes home, and the land thrives again.

versions.title: Agni Hides in the Waters
versions.teaser: The fire god, afraid of his job, slips away into the water.
versions.text:
Agni, the fire, is the gods' messenger and priest: every offering reaches heaven through his flames. In a dialogue hymn of the Rigveda (10.51), the gods find that he has vanished. He has slipped into the waters and the plants, wrapped in a thick membrane, afraid. His three elder brothers, he says, wore themselves out in the office of carrying the oblation, and he dreads the same fate.

The gods search and find him; Yama spots him, and the gods coax him. They offer terms: the first and last portions of the offering, the butter of the waters, the strength of the plants, and a long life. On those conditions Agni agrees to come back and carry the sacrifice again.

The later Taittirīya Saṃhitā adds an informer: a fish betrays Agni's hiding place, and Agni curses fish to be killed at will.
versions.caveat: Agni's absence starves the gods of sacrifice rather than blighting the land, so the fit with the pattern is only partial.

versions.title: Demeter on Strike
versions.teaser: The grain goddess sits alone in her temple, and nothing grows.
versions.text:
The Homeric Hymn to Demeter tells how the goddess, searching for her stolen daughter, turns away from Olympus in anger and grief. Disguised as an old woman, she takes a post as nurse in the house of King Celeus at Eleusis, and begins to make his baby son immortal by laying him in the fire at night, until his mother catches her at it and screams. Demeter reveals herself, demands a temple, and sits in it alone, mourning.

Then she stops the grain. For a whole year the earth sends up no seed, though oxen drag the curved ploughs across the fields and much white barley is sown in vain. The race of mortals would have perished, the hymn says, and the gods lost the honour of their offerings, had Zeus not taken notice. He sends the gods to her one after another with gifts; she refuses them all.

Only the return of Persephone ends the strike, and in thanks Demeter teaches the Eleusinians her mysteries.

versions.title: The Distant Goddess
versions.teaser: The sun's Eye storms off to Nubia, and must be charmed home.
versions.text:
The Eye of Ra is a goddess, often Tefnut or Hathor, and in a cycle of stories she quarrels with her father and goes off south into the Nubian desert. There she roams as a savage lioness, and Egypt is left without her. In the fullest version, the Demotic Myth of the Eye of the Sun from the Roman period, Thoth goes after her in the form of a little baboon and, with a long run of fables, flattery and argument, persuades her to come home.

Her journey north becomes a procession of joy. She is calmed with music and dancing, and the raging lioness turns into the gentle cat or the smiling Hathor. Temples along the Nile celebrated her homecoming, and Egyptologists have long linked it with the coming of the annual flood, which brought life back to the fields.
sources: Myth of the Eye of the Sun (Demotic, Papyrus Leiden I 384)
versions.caveat: The full narrative is late (Roman period), though the Distant Goddess theme is much older; the link to the Nile flood is scholarly inference.

versions.title: Endless Night on the High Plain
versions.teaser: The sun goddess withdraws, and darkness lets every calamity loose.
versions.text:
When Susanoo's outrages end in the death of one of her weaving maidens, Amaterasu withdraws into the Rock Cave of Heaven and shuts its door. The Kojiki dwells on what her absence does. The High Plain of Heaven goes dark, and so does the Central Land of Reed Plains below. Endless night reigns. The voices of the myriad spirits rise like swarming summer flies, and every kind of calamity breaks out at once.

The gods cannot simply wait her out. Eight hundred myriads of them gather in the bed of the Heavenly Tranquil River and set Omoikane, the god of thought, to devise a remedy; how the mirror, the dance and the laughter bring her out is told under 'The Sun Hidden Away'.

When the light returns, the gods settle the account. They fine Susanoo a thousand tables of offerings, cut off his beard and the nails of his fingers and toes, and drive him out of heaven.

versions.title: The Apples of Iðunn
versions.teaser: The keeper of youth is stolen, and the gods turn grey.
versions.text:
Iðunn keeps the apples that the gods eat to stay young. Loki, caught by the giant Þjazi in the shape of an eagle and dragged over stones and treetops, buys his freedom by promising to lure her out of Ásgarðr. He tells her he has found apples in a wood that she will think finer than her own, and she should bring hers to compare. Þjazi swoops down and carries her off to his home in Þrymheimr.

Without her, the gods quickly grow grey and old. They hold council, learn that Iðunn was last seen leaving with Loki, and threaten him with death or torture. Loki borrows Freyja's falcon shape, flies to Jötunheimr, turns Iðunn into a nut and carries her home in his claws. Þjazi pursues as an eagle, the gods light a fire of wood shavings at the wall, and the giant's feathers catch.

The world does not wither here; only the gods do. But it is the same shape of story, with the same cure.

concepts.summary: Why does the world warm and cool in a cycle instead of staying as it is? Many traditions answer with an arrangement: a god who must divide the year between two places, a sun who divides it between two wives, a dragon whose breath is summer and winter, a sky hole torn open to let the warmth through, or two fathers of different temper. The best-known Near Eastern and Greek versions build the seasons out of a bargain with the dead. All such stories explain what everyone can see; they differ in whether the cycle is a punishment, a compromise or simply the world's breathing.

versions.title: Brother and Sister Share the Year
versions.teaser: Dumuzi goes down for half the year, and his sister for the other half.
versions.text:
The Sumerian poem of Inanna's descent ends with a debt. Inanna, revived in the underworld, may leave only if she sends someone down in her place. Demons follow her up into the world, and in city after city her loyal servants and sons throw themselves at her feet in mourning, so she spares them. But in Kulaba she finds her husband Dumuzi seated on a high throne in splendid clothes, not grieving at all. She fixes on him the eye of death, and the demons seize him.

The damaged final lines, pieced together only in the 1960s, resolve the matter. Dumuzi's sister Geshtinanna, who loves him, offers to share his fate, and Inanna decrees: you for half the year, your sister for half the year. When he goes up, she goes down.

The shepherd and his sister, whose name contains the word for ‘vine’, divide the year between them, though which half belongs to whom the poem does not say.
versions.caveat: The half-year line is brief and was reconstructed from fragments; that it was meant to explain the seasons is a widely held inference, not a statement in the text.

versions.title: The Pomegranate Seed
versions.teaser: A seed eaten below means part of every year spent there.
versions.text:
Hades, with Zeus's consent, carries off Persephone as she picks flowers in a meadow. Her mother Demeter searches the earth with torches and, when she learns the truth, withholds the harvest until Zeus gives way and sends Hermes down to fetch the girl.

Hades lets her go graciously, but before she leaves he gives her a pomegranate seed, sweet as honey, and she eats it. Food of the dead binds the eater to them, and a compromise follows. In the Homeric Hymn, Persephone must spend a third of each year below with her husband and two thirds above with her mother and the gods; when the earth blooms with spring flowers, she rises. Later writers, Ovid among them, make it half and half.

The arithmetic has puzzled readers. Some scholars have argued that the hymn's barren season is the parched Greek summer, when the seed corn lay stored in underground jars, rather than a northern winter.

versions.title: The Torch Dragon's Breath
versions.teaser: A dragon's eyes make day and night; his breath makes winter and summer.
versions.text:
Beyond the northern seas, at the foot of Mount Zhong, lives the god Zhuyin, elsewhere called Zhulong, the Torch Dragon. The Classic of Mountains and Seas describes him in a handful of words: a human face, a serpent's body, red all over, a thousand li long. When he opens his eyes it is day; when he closes them it is night. When he blows out, it is winter; when he breathes out gently, it is summer. He neither drinks nor eats nor breathes, and when he does breathe, it is the wind.

The seasons here are not a story of loss and return but a physiology. The cycle of warmth and cold is one being's respiration, as regular as sleep and waking, and as far beyond human bargaining.

The Heavenly Questions of the Chuci ask where the sun does not reach, and how the Torch Dragon lights it. No answer is given.
sources: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Haiwai beijing and Dahuang beijing

versions.title: Rapithwin Goes Underground
versions.teaser: Winter is an attack, and the spirit of noon keeps the roots warm.
versions.text:
In Zoroastrian teaching, winter is not a natural phase but an assault. The first chapter of the Vendidad tells how Ahura Mazda created Airyana Vaējah, the first and best of lands, and how Angra Mainyu, the Evil Spirit, answered by creating a serpent in its river and a winter made by the demons: ten months of winter there, and two of summer.

Zoroastrian practice gave the warm season a guardian. Rapithwin, the spirit of noon and of summer, is honoured through the warm months with prayers at midday. When winter comes, he withdraws beneath the earth, where he keeps the roots of plants and the springs of water warm, so that they do not die. His return is celebrated with the coming of spring, and the noon prayers to him begin again.

The tradition holds that in the renovated world at the end of time, it will always be noon.
sources: Mary Boyce, A History of Zoroastrianism, vol. 1 (1975)
versions.caveat: The Rapithwin observance is described mainly from later Zoroastrian practice, as documented by Mary Boyce.

versions.title: Winter's Cold Father
versions.teaser: Summer and Winter are two persons of very different families.
versions.text:
In Vafþrúðnismál, Odin tests a wise giant with questions, and one of them is where winter and summer come from. The answer: Vindsvalr, ‘Wind-cool’, is Winter's father, and Svásuðr, ‘the Pleasant’, is Summer's. Snorri fills in their characters in Gylfaginning. Svásuðr and his whole line are gentle and delightful to live with, so that anything agreeable is named after him. Winter's kin, down from his father Vindsvalr, are grim and cold-hearted.

The same poem explains the wind: a giant in eagle form, Hræsvelgr, ‘Corpse-swallower’, sits at the end of heaven, and the wind comes from the beating of his wings.

This is seasonal change as family history rather than drama. No one is abducted and no bargain is struck. Winter and Summer are two persons of different descent, each behaving true to his blood, in a land where the difference between them could hardly be missed.

versions.title: Ojiig Brings the Summer
versions.teaser: The Fisher breaks a hole in the sky and lets the warmth down.
versions.text:
In a story Henry Rowe Schoolcraft printed in 1839 as ‘Ojeeg Annung, or the Summer-Maker’, the earth once knew only winter. A great hunter named Ojiig, the Fisher, lived with his wife and son. The boy wept because his fingers froze and he could catch nothing, and a squirrel told him that his father could bring the summer if he chose.

Ojiig agreed. With his animal friends, among them the otter, the beaver, the lynx and the wolverine, he climbed a high mountain until they could touch the sky. The wolverine leapt and broke through, and warm air and caged birds streamed down to earth. The sky people came running, and as Ojiig lingered to keep the opening wide, an arrow struck him in the tail, his one vulnerable spot. Dying, he was set among the stars.

The Fisher's stars, which others call the Big Dipper, wheel around the pole, and the warmth he stole is shared, part of the year, with the cold.
versions.caveat: Schoolcraft edited and embellished the stories he printed, so details may not match Ojibwe tellings.

versions.title: The Sun's Two Wives
versions.teaser: The sun divides his year between the Summer Maid and the Winter Maid.
versions.text:
In Māori tradition the sun, Tama-nui-te-rā, has two wives, and he divides the year between them. Hine-raumati, the Summer Maid, dwells on the land; Hine-takurua, the Winter Maid, dwells out on the ocean. While the sun stays with Hine-takurua he travels a low path and the days are short and cold. When he returns to Hine-raumati he climbs high across the sky, the land warms, and food plants grow.

The summer marriage has a child: Tāne-rore, whose dancing is the shimmer of heat above the ground on a hot day, and whom the haka is said to honour.

The story is not a tragedy. It is domestic, a husband's divided loyalties charted by the solstices, as precise in its way as an astronomer's table.
sources: Elsdon Best, The Maori Division of Time (1922)
versions.caveat: Recorded mainly by Elsdon Best from particular tribal experts; details vary among iwi.

concepts.summary: Nearly every mythology gives the dead a ruler, and the ruler's character says much about how a culture imagined death. Some are kings by lot or by marriage; some were the first to die and so found the road; some are judges, some jailers, some grim hosts. Yama in India and Yima in Iran descend from a shared Indo-Iranian figure, and Buddhism later carried Yama to China and Japan; other resemblances, such as the paired lord and lady of death in Mesoamerica and Mesopotamia, arose independently. Everywhere, the underworld has a government.

versions.title: Ereshkigal and Nergal
versions.teaser: The queen of the dead takes a husband by threatening to raise the dead.
versions.text:
Ereshkigal, ‘Lady of the Great Earth’, is queen of the land of no return, where the dead eat dust and clay and are clothed in feathers like birds. She cannot leave it to attend the gods' banquets, so they invite her to send a messenger, and she sends her vizier Namtar. Nergal alone fails to rise for him.

In the Akkadian poem Nergal and Ereshkigal, he must go down to make amends. Ea warns him to accept nothing below: no chair, no bread, no meat, no beer, no water for his feet, and, when the queen goes to bathe, not to give way to desire. He refuses the chair and the food, but not the queen. They lie together six days, and on the seventh he slips away.

Ereshkigal's message to the gods is a threat: send him back to be my husband, or I will raise the dead to eat the living. Nergal returns, seizes her by the hair, and the two rule the dead together.
sources: Nergal and Ereshkigal (Amarna and Sultantepe versions)
Descent of Ishtar to the Netherworld

versions.title: Osiris on the Throne
versions.teaser: The dead king judges every heart against a feather.
versions.text:
Osiris, murdered and restored, rules the Duat, and every Egyptian hoped to join him. Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead describes the test. The dead person enters the Hall of the Two Truths, where Osiris sits enthroned, wrapped as a mummy, his skin green or black like the fertile earth, holding the crook and flail. Before forty-two assessor gods, the deceased declares innocence of a long list of wrongs: I have not stolen, I have not killed, I have not tampered with the grain measure, I have not made anyone weep.

Then the heart is weighed on a balance against the feather of Maat, truth and right order. Anubis checks the scale and Thoth records the verdict. Beside it crouches Ammit, the Devourer, part crocodile, part lion, part hippopotamus, waiting for any heart that proves heavy.

The papyri were written in advance, and the vignettes show the verdict going the right way. Egypt's lord of the dead was a judge, but the dead brought their own acquittal.

image.caption: The weighing of the heart before Osiris, Papyrus of Hunefer, c. 1300 BCE (British Museum)

versions.title: Yama, King of the Fathers
versions.teaser: From feasting king of the fathers to buffalo-riding lord with a noose.
versions.text:
In the Rigveda, Yama is a king, and his realm is the best place the dead can hope for. The funeral hymn 10.14 sends the departed by the ancient paths to the highest heaven, to see the two kings, Yama and Varuṇa, rejoicing in the offerings, and to join the fathers there, leaving all blemish behind. Soma is pressed and butter offered to Yama himself, and another hymn (10.135) pictures him drinking with the gods beneath a fair-leaved tree. How he came to rule there, as the first to die, is told under 'How Death Entered the World'.

The Yama of the epics and Purāṇas is sterner. He is Dharmarāja, king of justice, ruling from his city in the south. Dark and riding a buffalo, he carries the staff of punishment and the noose with which he draws the soul from the dying, and his messengers fetch those whose time has come. Beside him the scribe Citragupta keeps the record of every deed.

The host of the fathers has become a magistrate.
versions.caveat: The buffalo, the noose and the scribe Citragupta belong to post-Vedic sources; the Rigvedic Yama is a host rather than a judge.

image.file: File:Yama on buffalo.jpg
image.caption: Yama, four-armed and blue-skinned, seated on his buffalo, Indian painting

versions.title: Hades and the Lots
versions.teaser: Three brothers draw lots, and the underworld falls to Hades.
versions.text:
In the Iliad, Poseidon recalls how the three sons of Cronus divided the world by lot. Zeus drew the broad sky, Poseidon the grey sea, and Hades the murky darkness below; the earth and high Olympus were left common to all. Hades, whose name the Greeks took to mean ‘the Unseen’, rules his share with his queen Persephone, seldom leaves it, and received very few temples.

His kingdom is grim more than cruel. When Odysseus summons the dead at the edge of the world, they crowd to drink the blood of his sacrifice, witless shades until they taste it. Achilles, greatest of the Greeks, tells him not to make light of death: he would rather be a hired labourer for a poor man on earth than king over all the perished dead.

To soften the name, the Greeks often called him Plouton, ‘the Rich’, lord of the wealth that comes up out of the ground.

versions.title: Izanami, Great Deity of Yomi
versions.teaser: The mother of the islands stays below and rules the dead.
versions.text:
When Izanami dies giving birth to fire, she goes down to Yomi, the land beneath, and there she stays. Her husband's failed attempt to bring her back is told under 'Bringing Back the Beloved Dead'; what matters here is what she becomes.

She has already eaten at the hearth of Yomi, and food of the dead binds the one who eats it. Her body is rotting, and eight thunder deities have been born from it. When Izanagi seals the slope between the worlds with a boulder, she makes the first great pronouncement of mortality: every day she will strangle a thousand people of his land. He answers that every day fifteen hundred will be born, and so the living stay ahead of the dead.

From then on she is called Yomotsu-ōkami, Great Deity of Yomi, and also Chishiki-no-ōkami, the deity who caught up with him. The boundary slope, the Kojiki adds, is Ifuya slope in Izumo.

versions.title: King Yama and the Ten Courts
versions.teaser: The Chinese underworld is a bureaucracy, with ledgers and a mirror.
versions.text:
Before Buddhism, the Chinese dead were imagined going to the Yellow Springs beneath the earth, or to Mount Tai in the east, whose god kept registers of the living and the dead. Buddhism brought a new ruler: Yama, the Indian lord of death, who became Yanluo Wang.

By the late Tang, the Scripture on the Ten Kings laid out an entire bureaucracy of judgement. The dead pass before ten kings in turn, at each of the first seven weeks after death, then at the hundredth day, the first year and the third year, each court staffed with clerks, ledgers and demon runners. Yama is the fifth king, and in his court the dead see their deeds reflected in a mirror and cannot lie. Families could lighten the sentence by sponsoring offerings and copying scripture at each stage.

In temple paintings the underworld kings sit in the robes of Chinese magistrates, behind desks. The Chinese afterlife, fittingly, has paperwork.
sources: Scripture on the Ten Kings (Shiwang jing)

versions.title: Hel's Hall
versions.teaser: Her plate is Hunger, her knife Famine, her bed Sick-bed.
versions.text:
When the gods learned what Loki's three children by the giantess Angrboða would become, Odin had them brought to him. The serpent he threw into the sea, the wolf the gods bound, and Hel he cast down into Niflheimr and gave her authority over nine worlds, to receive all who die of sickness or old age.

Snorri describes her household with bleak wit. Her hall is Éljúðnir, ‘Sleet-damp’; her plate is Hunger, her knife Famine; her servants are Ganglati and Ganglöt, both meaning ‘slow walker’; her threshold is Falling to Peril; her bed is Sick-bed and its hangings Gleaming Disaster. She herself is half black-blue and half flesh-coloured, easily recognised, and rather grim and fierce in her looks.

In the poems hel is as much a place as a person, the common home of the dead, reached by a road that runs down and north, over the echoing bridge Gjallarbrú.
