image.caption: Hel on a cliff ledge with a hound, Johannes Gehrts, 1889

versions.title: The Lords of Xibalba
versions.teaser: A whole court of death gods, vain, cruel and easily fooled.
versions.text:
Xibalba, the ‘Place of Fear’ in the Popol Vuh, has not one lord of death but a council. At its head sit One Death and Seven Death, and beneath them paired lords with telling names: Pus Demon and Jaundice Demon, Bone Scepter and Skull Scepter, Bloody Teeth and Bloody Claws, Wing and Packstrap, who make people swell, waste, bleed, or collapse on the road.

The lords are vain and easily offended, and the noise of ballplayers above their heads is reason enough to summon them below. They test their visitors with tricks: wooden manikins seated among them to be greeted by mistake, a bench that is really a burning stone, and houses of darkness, cold, jaguars, bats and blades.

They are also gullible. The Hero Twins, disguised as wandering performers, dazzle them by sacrificing and reviving each other. One Death and Seven Death beg to be sacrificed and revived in turn. The Twins oblige with the first half only, and Xibalba's power is broken.

versions.title: Mictlantecuhtli and the Bones
versions.teaser: The lord of the dead guards the bones from which humans are remade.
versions.text:
Mictlantecuhtli, ‘Lord of Mictlan’, rules the deepest level of the underworld with his consort Mictecacihuatl. In the painted books he is a skeleton spattered with blood, sometimes with his liver hanging beneath his ribs.

The Legend of the Suns tells how he was outwitted. After the previous world is destroyed, Quetzalcoatl goes down to Mictlan to fetch the precious bones of the earlier people, so that the gods can make humans again. Mictlantecuhtli agrees on a condition: Quetzalcoatl must blow a conch trumpet and circle his realm four times. The conch has no holes, so Quetzalcoatl calls worms to bore them and bees to fly inside and make it sound. The lord then has a pit dug; startled by quail, Quetzalcoatl falls, and the bones scatter and break, and the quail peck at them. He gathers them anyway and escapes.

The goddess Quilaztli grinds the bones, the gods bleed on them, and humankind is made from broken bones and divine blood.
sources: Legend of the Suns (Leyenda de los Soles, 1558)

image.caption: Page 56 of the Codex Borgia, a pre-Columbian ritual book from central Mexico

versions.title: Tuoni's River
versions.teaser: A guest in Tuonela is offered frog beer and an iron net.
versions.text:
Tuonela, the Finnic land of the dead, lies across a black river, and its rulers are Tuoni and his wife Tuonetar. In the Kalevala, Väinämöinen goes there alive to look for the three words he lacks. Tuoni's daughter, a small, stunted girl washing clothes at the river, asks why he has come before his time. He lies about how he died, and she sees through each lie, until he tells the truth and she ferries him over.

Tuonetar greets him with a tankard of beer in which frogs and worms are writhing. He will not drink. He is lulled to sleep, and Tuoni's son, an old man with iron fingers, weaves a net of iron and copper across the river so that the guest can never leave.

Väinämöinen escapes by turning himself into an iron serpent and slipping through the mesh. Back home, he warns his people never to go to Tuonela before their time: many have gone there, and few have come back.
versions.caveat: The Kalevala is Elias Lönnrot's nineteenth-century compilation from folk songs.

image.caption: By the River of Tuonela, study for the Jusélius Mausoleum frescoes, Akseli Gallen-Kallela, c. 1903

concepts.summary: The journey from death to the other world is usually too dangerous to make alone, so traditions provide a guide: a god who knows the roads, a ferryman at the river, a dog, a maiden, a band of warrior women, a gaunt driver with a cart. The Greek word psychopompos, ‘leader of souls’, names the role. Some guides may share an inheritance (Vedic Pūṣan has been compared with Greek Pan, though the link is uncertain), but most reflect an almost universal image of death as a journey that needs a pathfinder, a vehicle or a crossing.

versions.title: Ferrymen of the Dead
versions.teaser: A boatman across the Waters of Death, and one named ‘Take away quickly’.
versions.text:
Mesopotamian sources know two ferrymen. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, Urshanabi, boatman of Utnapishtim, carries Gilgamesh across the Waters of Death, where a single drop on the skin would kill. Gilgamesh has smashed the ‘Stone Ones’ who normally help Urshanabi cross, so he must cut hundreds of punting poles and throw each one away as soon as it is wet; when they run out, he strips off his garment and holds it up as a sail.

For the ordinary dead, the way lay across the underworld river Hubur. In a Neo-Assyrian text known as the Underworld Vision of an Assyrian Prince, a prince named Kummaya dreams of Ereshkigal's realm and sees its monstrous officials. Among them is Humut-tabal, ferryman of the netherworld, with the head of the Anzu bird and four hands and feet. His name is an order: ‘Take away quickly’.
sources: Underworld Vision of an Assyrian Prince

versions.title: Anubis Takes the Hand
versions.teaser: The jackal god embalms the dead, then leads them to judgement.
versions.text:
Anubis, the jackal-headed god, embalmed Osiris, and so became the patron of every mummy. In tomb paintings and Book of the Dead papyri he appears at each stage of the passage. He leans over the bier to tend the body; he holds the mummy upright at the tomb door for the Opening of the Mouth; and, most memorably, he takes the dead person by the hand and leads him into the hall of judgement, then kneels at the great balance to see that the heart and the feather of Maat are weighed truly.

One of his titles, ‘He who is upon his mountain’, sets him on the cliffs above the desert cemeteries, where real jackals prowled; Egyptians seem to have made the scavenger of graves into their guardian. A second canine god, Wepwawet, ‘Opener of the Ways’, went ahead of the king in procession and of the dead on the roads of the west.

image.caption: Anubis supports the mummy of Hunefer at the Opening of the Mouth, Papyrus of Hunefer, c. 1300 BCE (British Museum)

versions.title: Pūṣan Knows the Roads
versions.teaser: The toothless herdsman god who never loses a cow leads the dead.
versions.text:
Pūṣan is a modest Vedic god: a herdsman who eats gruel because he has no teeth, drives a car drawn by goats, and carries a goad. His particular gift is finding: lost cattle, lost ways, the right road for a traveller. He knows all the paths.

That makes him a guide for the dead. The funeral hymn Rigveda 10.17 asks him to lead the departed onward: may Pūṣan, the knowing herdsman of the world, whose cattle are never lost, conduct you from here and hand you over to the fathers. Pūṣan knows all these regions, the hymn continues, and will lead us by the least perilous way, going first, watchful and wise.

In the horse sacrifice (Rigveda 1.162) a goat, Pūṣan's share, is led before the horse to announce it to the gods. Some scholars have linked Pūṣan's name with that of Greek Pan, another goatish god of herds and paths, but the connection remains uncertain.

versions.title: Hermes and Charon
versions.teaser: Hermes leads the gibbering dead; Charon poles them across.
versions.text:
The last book of the Odyssey opens with a grim procession. Hermes of Cyllene, holding his golden wand, calls out the souls of Penelope's slaughtered suitors, and they follow him gibbering, like bats squeaking in the depths of a cave when one drops from the cluster. He leads them down the dank ways, past the streams of Ocean and the White Rock, past the gates of the Sun and the land of dreams, to the meadow of asphodel where the dead dwell. Hence his title psychopompos, ‘leader of souls’.

At the edge of the underworld waits Charon, a surly old boatman who is absent from Homer but familiar by the fifth century BCE, poling the dead across the marsh. On Athenian white-ground lekythoi, oil flasks placed with the dead, Hermes delivers a shade to Charon's boat. Some Greeks put a coin, an obol, in the corpse's mouth to pay the fare.

image.caption: Hermes leads a woman to Charon's boat, white-ground lekythos by the Sabouroff Painter, mid-5th century BCE (National Archaeological Museum, Athens)

versions.title: The Maiden at the Bridge
versions.teaser: At the Chinvat Bridge, each soul meets the self it has made.
versions.text:
In Zoroastrian teaching the soul lingers by the body for three nights after death. At the dawn after the third night it comes to the Chinvat Bridge, the ‘Bridge of the Separator’, over which the way leads to paradise.

There it meets its own daēnā, its religious self, in bodily form. To a righteous soul, the Avestan Hadōxt Nask says, she comes on a fragrant wind from the south, a beautiful maiden of fifteen, radiant, white-armed and tall. Who are you? the soul asks. She answers that she is his own daēnā: she was lovely, and he made her lovelier by his good thoughts, good words and good deeds. She leads him across, and the bridge is broad beneath his feet.

The wicked soul meets a foul wind from the north and, in the Pahlavi texts, a hideous hag; for it the bridge narrows to a blade's edge, and it falls into the House of the Lie. The guide is the self one has made.

versions.title: The Paddler Gods' Canoe
versions.teaser: Two old gods paddle the maize god into the watery underworld.
versions.text:
Among the offerings in Burial 116 at Tikal, the tomb of the eighth-century king Jasaw Chan K'awiil, were bones incised with fine drawings. One shows a canoe gliding on the water, steered by two old gods, the Paddlers, one at the prow and one at the stern. Between them sit the young maize god and a cargo of animals, an iguana, a monkey, a parrot, a dog, some raising a hand to the face in what looks like lament. On a companion bone the canoe is shown sinking, prow first, into the water.

Mayanists usually read the scene as the passage of the dead king, in the guise of the maize god, into the watery underworld, from which he would rise renewed. The Paddlers themselves, the Jaguar Paddler and the Stingray Paddler, appear in inscriptions as gods present at the creation of the present world.
sources: Incised bones from Tikal Burial 116 (8th c.)
versions.caveat: The reading of the canoe as a journey of the dead interprets imagery; no surviving Maya text narrates it.

versions.title: The Choosers of the Slain
versions.teaser: Valkyries ride out to choose the dead and bring them to Valhöll.
versions.text:
Valkyries, the ‘choosers of the slain’, ride over battlefields to decide who will fall, and they bring the chosen dead to Odin's hall, Valhöll. In the tenth-century poem Eiríksmál, composed for the dead king Eiríkr Blood-axe, Odin wakes before dawn, orders the benches readied and the valkyries to bring wine, because a king is coming. In Hákonarmál, Odin sends two valkyries to choose King Hákon the Good; one of them speaks to him on the battlefield, and they ride ahead to announce him.

Snorri adds that in Valhöll they serve drink to the einherjar, the warrior dead, and Grímnismál names several, among them Hildr, ‘Battle’, and Skögul.

Not every guide rode a horse. At the funeral of a Rus chieftain on the Volga in 922, the Arab envoy Ibn Faḍlān saw an old woman called the ‘Angel of Death’ lead a slave girl to die beside her master.
versions.caveat: Ibn Faḍlān's Rus were Scandinavians in the east, but how far their rites reflect belief elsewhere in the Norse world is debated.

versions.title: The Road to Mictlan
versions.teaser: Papers for every peril, and a dog for the last river.
versions.text:
The ordinary dead, those who had not died in battle, in childbirth or by water, set out on a four-year road to Mictlan, as Sahagún's Nahua informants described it. The mourners equipped them for it. Cut papers were laid with the body, each meant to carry the dead past one danger: the two mountains that clash together, the road guarded by a serpent, the green lizard, the eight deserts and eight hills, and the wind of obsidian blades. The dead person's clothes and goods were burned so the cold wind would not cut so deep.

The companion for the road was a dog, killed and cremated with its master. At the last river it swims across carrying him, as told under 'The Hound at Death's Gate'.

At the end, the dead come before Mictlantecuhtli and give him the papers, incense and cloth they carried. After four years they reach the ninth place of the dead, and there they end.
versions.caveat: Recorded in the sixteenth century, after the Conquest, by Sahagún and his Nahua collaborators.

versions.title: The Ankou
versions.teaser: Death's cart creaks through Brittany at night, with a backward scythe.
versions.text:
In Lower Brittany the Ankou is death's workman. In each parish, the last person to die in the year becomes its Ankou for the year that follows. People who heard the creak of his cart at night, the karrigell an Ankou, knew that a death was near.

Anatole Le Braz, who collected Breton death legends in the 1890s, describes him as a tall, gaunt figure, sometimes a skeleton, in a long coat and a broad-brimmed hat, with long white hair, carrying a scythe whose blade is fixed facing outward, so that he swings it forward instead of drawing it toward him. Two companions walk with the cart, one leading the horse, one opening the gates of fields and houses. Where he stops, someone dies.

The Ankou belongs to Catholic Brittany, and churches carve him on ossuaries and fonts. Whether any pre-Christian figure lies behind him, no one can say.
sources: Anatole Le Braz, La Légende de la mort chez les Bretons armoricains (1893)
versions.caveat: A folk figure of the Christian era; claims of a pre-Christian Celtic origin are speculative.
